translations.title: Ballad of My Name
translations.text:
The name of mine that I have lost,

where does it live, where does it thrive?

A childhood name, a drop of milk,

a myrtle branch so light.


Had it not carried me, I would have gone gladly,

or carried my adolescence;

and with it I no longer walk

through fields and meadows.


It knows no weeping of mine,

nor has my brine burned it;

it has not seen my hair turn white,

nor my mouth grow weary,

and it does not speak to me when it finds me.


But they tell me it walks

through the ravines of my mountain,

quietly, evening after evening,

without my body, my soul made over.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Circle of Girls
translations.text:
Circle of girls,
a circle of a thousand girls
around me:
O God, I am mistress
of this radiance!


On the barren earth,
over that desert
bitten by the sun,
my circle of girls
like an immense flower!


On the green plain,
at the foot of the mountains
that the voice struck,
the circle was one
single divine trembling!


On the immense steppe,
on the desolate steppe
of desolation,
my circle of girls
ablaze with love!


In vain they tried
to break my stanza
with tribulation:
the circle sings it
beneath God's care!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Two Angels
translations.text:
I have not just one Angel
with a quivering wing:
the Angel who gives joy
and the one who gives agony
rock me as the two shores
rock the sea,
the one with fluttering wings
and the one with wings held still.


I know, when dawn comes,
which one will rule my day,
whether the flame-colored one
or the ash-colored one,
and I give myself to them,
contrite, like seaweed to a wave.


Only once did they fly
with their wings joined:
on the day of love,
the day of Epiphany.


They joined their enemy wings
into a single pair,
and tied the knot
of death and life!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: A Rat Chased a Deer...
translations.text:
A rat chased a deer,
and the deer chased the jaguar,
and the jaguars chased the buffalo,
and the buffalo chased the sea…


Catch them, catch them, those who flee!
Catch the rat, catch the deer,
catch the buffalo and the sea!


Look, the leading rat carries
embroidery wool in its paws,
and with that wool I'll embroider my dress,
and in that dress I'll marry.


Climb up and cross the plain,
run breathless, keep on without stopping.
Fly for the bride, and for the wedding party,
for the carriage and the bridal veil.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: He Passed with Another...
translations.text:
He passed with another;
I saw him pass.
The wind was always gentle
and the road at peace.
And these wretched eyes
saw him pass!


He goes loving another
across the blossoming earth.
The thorn tree has opened;
a song goes by.
And he goes loving another
across the blossoming earth!


He kissed the other
beside the sea;
on the waves slipped
the orange-blossom moon.
And the wide sea's reach
did not anoint my blood!


He will go with another
through eternity.
Sweet heavens will be there.
(God grant that He be silent.)
And he will go with another
through eternity!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Those Who Do Not Dance
translations.text:
A girl who was disabled
said, “How can I dance?”
We told her to set
her heart dancing…


Then the stream said,
“How could I sing?”
We told it to set
its heart singing…


The poor dead thistle said,
“How could I dance?”
We told it, “Set your heart
to flying on the wind…”


God spoke from on high:
“How do I come down from blue?”
We told Him to come down
and dance for us in the light.


The whole valley is dancing
in a circle beneath the sun,
and for anyone who will not join,
the heart becomes earth, earth.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Mother, Mother, You Kiss Me...
translations.text:
Mother, Mother, you kiss me,
but I kiss you more,
and the swarm of my kisses
will not even let you look…


When the bee enters the lily,
its fluttering cannot be heard.
When you hide your little one,
even his breathing is unheard…


I look at you, I look at you,
never tired of looking,
and what a lovely child I see
appearing in your eyes…


The pond copies all
that you are looking at;
but in your little girls you have
your son and nothing else.


The little eyes you gave me
I must wear away
following you through valleys,
through sky and sea…
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Little Hands
translations.text:
Little hands of children,
little begging hands,
of the world's valleys
you are the queens.


Little hands of children
reaching toward the pomegranate tree,
for your sake the fruits
light up.


And the honeycombs, full,
are burdened by their load.
And the people passing by
do not understand!


White little hands, made
as if of soft flour,
the grain bends down
to touch you.


Outstretched little hands,
pine nuts, little snails,
blessed be whoever fills them,
blessed!


Blessed are those who, hearing
you seem to cry out,
return you to the world:
blessed!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Song of Fisherwomen
translations.text:
Little fisherman's girl,
you can keep pace with wind and waves;
sleep, painted with shells,
sketched over with nets.


Sleep atop the dune
that lifts you and grows you,
hearing the sea-nurse,
who rocks all the wilder for it.


The net fills my skirt
and will not let me hold you,
for if I break the knots,
I will break your fate…


Sleep better than those
who rock in their cradles,
with mouths full of salt
and dreams full of fish.


Two fish on your knees,
one silver one on your brow,
and on your chest, beating, beating,
another incandescent fish…
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Give Me Your Hand
translations.text:
Give me your hand and we will dance;
give me your hand and you will love me.
We will be like a single flower,
like one flower, and nothing more…


We will sing the same verse,
you will dance in the same step.
We will sway like a stalk of wheat,
like one stalk, and nothing more.


Your name is Rose and mine is Hope;
but you will forget your name,
for we will be one dance
on the hillside and nothing more…


Author's note: My companion, the poet Tasso de
Silveira, rescued for me a lost stanza from this Round,
the only one perhaps worth preserving, which had
been removed by an editor or typesetter…
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Snow Has Come Down, Divine Creature...
translations.text:
The snow has come down, divine creature,
to know the valley.
The snow has come down, lovelier than the stars.
Let us watch it fall!


It comes, hush-hush, falling and falling at the doors,
and knocks without knocking.
So the Virgin comes, and so dreams arrive.
Let us watch it come!


She loosens the great nest in the heavens
and makes it fly.
Feathers fall on the valley, feathers on the plain,
feathers on the olive grove.


Perhaps, falling and falling, it broke
the message of Our Lord God.
Perhaps it was His cloak, perhaps His image,
perhaps only His love.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Parrot
translations.text:
The green-and-yellow parrot,
the green-and-saffron parrot,
called me “ugly” in its nasal speech
and with its beak from Satan.


I am not ugly; if I were ugly,
my mother would be ugly, like the sun;
the light my mother looks into would be ugly,
and ugly the wind where she sets her voice,
and ugly the water where her body falls,
and ugly the world, and He who made it…


The green-and-yellow parrot,
the green-and-iridescent parrot,
called me “ugly” because it has not eaten,
and I bring it bread and wine,
for I am growing tired of looking at it,
always hanging there, always iridescent…
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Little Eyes of the Stars...
translations.text:
Little eyes of the stars,
opened in dark
velvet: from on high,
do you see me pure?


Little eyes of the stars,
kindled in the serene
sky, tell me: from above,
do you see me good?


Little eyes of the stars,
with restless little lashes,
why are you blue, red,
and violet?


Little eyes of the curious
pupil, awake all night,
why does the dawn erase you
with its roses?


Little eyes, spatters
of tears or dew,
when you tremble up there,
is it from cold?


Little eyes of the stars,
fixed on one and another, I swear
you will always look at me,
always pure.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Three Trees
translations.text:
Three fallen trees
remained beside the path.
The woodcutter forgot them, and they talk,
pressed close in love, like three blind men.


The setting sun lays
its living blood on the split logs,
and the winds carry away
the fragrance of their open side!


One, twisted, stretches
its immense arm of trembling foliage
toward the other, and its wounds
are like two eyes, full of pleading.


The woodcutter forgot them. Night
will come. I will be with them.


I will receive their gentle
resins in my heart. They will be like fire to me.
And silent, pressed close,
may day find us in a heap of grief!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: To See Him Again
translations.text:
And never, never again, not in nights filled
with the trembling of stars, nor in virgin
dawns, nor in sacrificed evenings?


Not beside any pale path
that girdles the field, beside no
quivering fountain, white with moonlight?


Not beneath the forest's braided boughs,
where night has overtaken me calling him,
nor in the cave that echoes my cry?


Oh, no! To see him again, wherever it may be,
in heaven's still pools or a boiling whirlpool,
beneath calm moons or in a purple horror!


And to be with him through every spring
and every winter, in an anguished
knot around his bloodied neck!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Evil Hands Took Your Life from the Day
translations.text:
Evil hands took your life from the day
you left your snow-covered bed of lilies
at a sign from the stars. It was flowering in joy.
Evil hands entered it with tragedy…


And I said to the Lord: “They lead him along
the mortal paths. Beloved shadow, they cannot guide!
Tear him, Lord, from those fatal hands,
or sink him into the long sleep You know how to give!


“I cannot shout to him, I cannot follow him!
A black storm wind drives his boat.
Bring him back to my arms, or cut him down in bloom.”


The rose boat of his life came to a halt…
Did I not know love, did I have no pity?
You who will judge me, You understand, Lord!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: This Long Weariness
translations.text:
This long weariness will grow greater one day,
and the soul will tell the body it will not go on
dragging its weight along the rosy road
where men go, glad to be alive…


You will feel them digging vigorously beside you,
feel another sleeper come to the quiet city.
I will wait until they have covered me completely…
and then we will speak for all eternity!


Only then will you know why your flesh,
not yet ripe for the deep graves,
had to come down, without weariness, to sleep.
Light will break in the dark region of destinies:
you will know our bond bore a sign from the stars,
and, the great pact broken, you had to die…
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: From the Icy Niche Where Men Put You
translations.text:
From the icy niche where men placed you,
I will lower you to the humble, sunlit earth.
They did not know I would sleep there too,
and that we would dream on the same pillow.


I will lay you in the sunny earth
with a mother's sweetness for her sleeping child,
and the earth will grow soft as a cradle
as it receives your sorrowing child's body.


Then I will sprinkle earth and rose dust,
and in the light blue, gentle moon-dust,
your light remains will be held fast.


I will go away singing my beautiful vengeance,
for into that hidden depth no woman's hand
will descend to contest your handful of bones with me!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Mother, When I Am Grown...
translations.text:
Mother, when I am grown,
oh, what a strapping lad you'll have!
I'll lift you in my arms,
as the zonda lifts the grass.


Or I'll lay you on the haystacks,
or carry you all the way to the sea,
or take you up the hills,
or leave you on the threshold.


And what a little home will
your little boy, your giant, build for you,
and what loving shade
its eaves will give?


I'll water you a garden,
and tire your skirt out
with fruit and more fruit,
a thousand kinds and more.


Or better, I'll make you tapestries
from rushes for weaving;
or better, I'll own a mill
to talk to you as it makes bread.


Count, count the windows
and the doors of the house;
count, count the wonders,
if you can count them…
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Fear
translations.text:
I do not want them to turn my little girl
into a swallow;
she flies up into Heaven
and does not come down to my mat;
she nests beneath the eaves,
and my hands cannot comb her.
I do not want them to turn my little girl
into a swallow.


I do not want them to make my little girl
a princess.
With little golden shoes,
how could she play in the meadows?
And when night comes,
she will not lie down beside me…
I do not want them to make my little girl
a princess.


Still less do I want one day
to see them make her a queen.
They would raise her to a throne
where my feet cannot reach.
When night came,
I could not rock her…
I do not want them to make my little girl
my queen!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Earth and the Woman
translations.text:
While the world still has light
and my child is awake,
over his face
everything winks at him.


The grove winks at him
with its yellow fingers,
and behind it come the clouds
in little goat-like somersaults…


At noon the cicada
winks with its rubbing,
and the breeze's slyness
winks with its little diaper.


When night comes,
the cricket winks slyly,
and when the stars appear,
their holy little winks will reach him…


I tell the other Mother,
the one filled with roads:
“Make your little one sleep,
so mine will fall asleep!”


And that indulgent one,
striped with roads,
answers me: “Put yours to sleep,
so mine will fall asleep!”
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: When I Heard a Cry, I Stopped on the Rise...
translations.text:
When I heard a cry, I stopped on the rise
and went to the door of the roadside hut.
A child with gentle eyes looked at me from his bed.
And an immense tenderness intoxicated me like wine!


The mother was late, bent over the fallow field;
when the child awoke, he searched for the rose's nipple
and burst into tears… I held him against my breast,
and a lullaby rose from me, trembling…


The moon watched us through the open window.
The child was already asleep, and the song bathed,
like another radiance, my heart made rich…


And when the woman, trembling, opened the door,
she must have seen such certain joy on my face
that she left the infant sleeping in my arms!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: I Sing What You Loved
translations.text:
I sing what you loved, my life,
in case you come near and listen, my life,
in case you remember the world you lived in;
at dusk I sing, my shadow.


I do not want to fall silent, my life.
How would you find me without my faithful cry?
What sign, what mark would tell you, my life?


I am the same woman who was yours, my life.
Neither slow nor forgetful nor lost.
Come at nightfall, my life;
come remembering a song, my life,
if you recognize the song you learned,
and if you still remember my name.


I wait for you without deadline or time.
Fear neither night, nor fog, nor downpour.
Come by a path or without a path.
Call me where you are, my soul,
and walk straight toward me, companion.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Hide Me
translations.text:
Hide me, so the world will not guess me.
Hide me as the trunk hides its resin, and
let me perfume you in the shade, like
a drop of gum; let me soften you with
it, so the others will not know where
your sweetness comes from…


I am ugly without you, like things torn
from their place; like roots abandoned
on the ground.


Why am I not small as an almond
inside its closed shell?


Drink me! Make me a drop of your blood,
and I will rise to your cheek and live there
like the vivid speck on a grape leaf.
Make me your sigh, and I will rise
and fall from your chest, wind myself
around your heart, go out into the air and return.
And I will play this game
all my life.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The One-Armed Girl
translations.text:
My little finger, a clam caught it,
and the clam fell into the sand,
and the sand swallowed it in the sea.
And from the sea a whaler fished it up,
and the whaler reached Gibraltar;
and in Gibraltar the fishermen sing:
“News from the land we brought out of the sea,
news of a little girl's finger:
let the one who's missing one come claim it!”


Give me a ship so I can go fetch it,
and give the ship a captain,
and give the captain his wages,
and for wages he asks for the city:
Marseille, with its towers and squares and ships,
the finest city in all the world,
which will not be beautiful with a little girl
whose finger the sea stole,
while the whalers sing their cries
and wait above Gibraltar…
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: This Fearful, Sad Water...
translations.text:
This fearful, sad water,
like a suffering child,
faints before it even
touches the earth.


The tree is still, the wind still,
and in the awesome silence,
this fine, bitter weeping
falls!


The sky is like an immense
heart opening, bitterly.
It is not rain: it is a slow,
long bleeding.


Inside the home, people
do not feel this bitterness,
this sending of sad water
from above.


This long, exhausting
descending of defeated waters
toward the Earth, lying down
and stricken.


It rains… and like a tragic jackal
night waits in the mountains.
What will rise in the shadows
from the Earth?


Will you sleep while outside
this lifeless water falls, suffering,
this lethal water, sister
to Death?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Coplas
translations.text:
Everything takes on in my mouth
a lasting taste of tears:
the daily meal, the song,
even prayer.


I have no other trade,
after the silent work of loving you,
than this hard trade of tears
you left me.


Eyes squeezed shut
with hot tears!
Troubled, convulsed mouth,
where everything becomes a prayer!


I am ashamed
to live this cowardly way!
I neither go in search of you
nor can I forget you!


Remorse bleeds me
when I look at a sky
your eyes cannot see,
when I touch the roses
nourished by the lime of your bones!


Flesh of misery,
shameful, weary branch,
that will not lie down beside you,
that presses, trembling,
to Life's impure breast!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Flower of the Air
translations.text:
I found her there, by my destiny,
standing in the middle of the meadow,
ruler of whoever passes,
whoever speaks to her, whoever sees her.


And she said to me, “Climb the mountain.
I never leave the meadow,
and cut me white flowers,
hard and tender as snow.”


I climbed the bitter mountain,
searched for the flowers whitening there,
existing among the rocks,
half asleep and half awake.


When I came down with my burden,
I found her in the middle of the meadow,
and covered her frantically
with a flood of lilies.


Without looking at their whiteness,
she said to me, “Now bring me
only red flowers.
I cannot cross the meadow.”


I climbed the crags with the deer
and searched for flowers of madness,
those that redden and seem
to live and die by their redness.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: If You Look at Me, I Become Beautiful...
translations.text:
If you look at me, I grow beautiful
like grass touched by dew,
and the tall reeds will not know
my glorious face when I go down to the river.


I am ashamed of my sad mouth,
my broken voice and my rough knees;
now that you looked at me and came,
I found myself poor and felt myself naked.


You found no stone along the road
more stripped of light at dawn
than this woman you lifted up,
because you heard her song, and looked.


I will be silent, so those crossing the plain
will not know my joy,
in the glow that falls on my rough brow,
in the trembling of my hand…


It is night, and dew descends on the grass;
look at me long and speak tenderly,
so that tomorrow, when I go down to the river,
what you kissed will bear beauty!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Serene Words
translations.text:
Now, halfway through my days, I gather
this truth, fresh as a flower:
life is gold and the sweetness of wheat,
hatred is brief and love immense.


Let us trade for the smiling verse
that old roll of blood and gall.
Divine violets open, and the wind
breathes a honey scent down to the valley.


Now I understand not only the one who prays;
now I understand the one who breaks into song.
Thirst is long, the slope is crooked;
but the gaze catches on a lily.


Our eyes are heavy with tears,
yet a little stream makes us smile;
for a lark raising its song
we forget how hard it is to die.


Nothing now pierces my flesh.
Love has ended the boiling within.
My mother's gaze still feeds me.
I feel God lulling me to sleep!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Lady Spring
translations.text:
Lady Spring
is dressed so fine,
dressed in lemon trees
and orange trees in bloom.


She wears broad leaves
for sandals,
and bright red fuchsias
for earrings.


Go out to meet her
along those roads.
She is wild with sunshine
and wild with birdsong!


Lady Spring,
with her fertile breath,
laughs at all
the world's sorrows…


She will not believe anyone
who tells her of wretched lives.
How could she meet them
among the jasmine?


How could she find them
beside the fountains,
with their golden mirrors
and ardent songs?


From the sick earth's
brown cracks,
she kindles rosebushes
in red pirouettes.


She lays down her lace,
sets her greenery alight
on the sad stone
of the graves…


Lady Spring,
of glorious hands,
make us scatter roses
throughout our lives:


Roses of joy,
roses of pardon,
roses of affection,
and of exultation.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: I Love, Love
translations.text:
It roams free in the furrow, beats its wing in the wind,
pulses alive in the sun and clings to the pine grove.
You cannot forget it as you would an evil thought:
you will have to listen to it!


It speaks a tongue of bronze and a bird's tongue,
timid pleas, the sea's commands.
You cannot put on a bold face, a solemn frown:
you will have to shelter it!


It bears the airs of a master; excuses cannot soften it.
It shatters flower-cups, cleaves the deep glacier.
You cannot tell it you refuse to harbor it:
you will have to shelter it!


It has subtle tricks in its clever replies,
a scholar's arguments, but in a woman's voice.
Human knowledge may save you, but not divine knowledge:
you will have to believe it!


It ties a linen blindfold on you; you let it stay.
It offers its warm arm; you cannot flee it.
It starts walking, and you follow, spellbound, though you know
this road ends in death!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Farewell
translations.text:
On a distant shore
and in a sea of Passion,
we said our farewells
without saying goodbye.
And the vision
was not true.
Neither did you believe it
nor do I,
“it is true and it is not true,”
as in the song.

As I went south,
I kept saying:
“Let us go to the sea
that devours the Sun.”
And as you went north,
your voice said:
“Let us go together
to see where the Sun is born.”

Do not say, even in jest
or in exaggeration,
that earth and sea separated us,
the earth and sea that are
its dream and
its delirium.

Do not call yourself alone,
nor let your voice ask
the host for shelter
for just one.
You will cast the shadow
we have always cast,
you will bite the dune
with two people's tread…

So no one,
neither man nor god,
will call us divided
like moon and sun;
so neither rock
nor wandering wind,
nor fordable river
nor shading tree,
will learn to speak
lie or error
of South and North,
of one and two!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Thorn Tree
translations.text:
The thorn tree fastens to a rock
its frenzied contortion,
and is the spirit of the wasteland,
twisted with anguish and sun.


The oak is beautiful as Jupiter,
and the flowering myrtle is a Narcissus.
They made this one like Vulcan,
the dreadful forging god.


They made it without the lacy grace
of the bright, trembling poplar,
so the traveler's soul
would never know its pain.


Flowers grow from its shaggy crown.
(So Job's verse was born.)
And like the leper's psalm,
its intense pain is sharp.


Though it fills the blazing air
of midday with its scent,
its dark tangled crown has never felt
a nest tremble within it…


It told me that it knows me,
that on a night of pain,
in its dense million thorns,
my heart was bruised.


I embraced it like a sister,
as if Hagar embraced Job,
in a clasp that is not tenderness,
but something more: despair!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Absence
translations.text:
My body leaves you drop by drop.
My face goes in a muted wash of oil;
my hands go in loose quicksilver;
my feet go in two measures of dust.


Everything leaves you, everything leaves us!


My voice goes, the voice that made a bell for you,
closed to all that is not us.
My gestures go, winding themselves
like shuttles before your eyes.
And the gaze goes that gave you,
when it looked at you, the juniper and elm.


I leave you with the very breath you breathe:
I evaporate like moisture from your body.
I leave you awake and asleep,
and in your most faithful memory I already fade.
In your mind I become like those
who were born neither in plains nor groves.


I would be blood, flowing from the palms
of your labor and your mouth of must.
I would be your entrails, burning
on your journeys I no longer hear,
and in your passion thundering at night,
like the madness of lonely seas!


Everything leaves us, everything leaves us!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Other One
translations.text:
I killed one in me:
I did not love her.


She was the flaming flower
of the mountain cactus;
she was aridity and fire;
she never cooled herself.


She had stone and sky
at her feet and her back,
and never came down
to search for “eyes of water.”


Where she took her siesta,
grasses curled up
from the breath of her mouth
and the ember of her face.


Her speech hardened
into quick resins,
so as not to fall into
a lovely, loosened snare.


The mountain plant
did not know how to bend,
and beside her,
I would bend…


I let her die,
stealing my own entrails from her.
She ended like an eagle
that is not fed.


Her wingbeat quieted,
she bent, limp,
and her spent cinder
fell into my hand…


For her, her sisters
still moan to me,
and the fiery clays
tear at me as I pass.


As I cross, I tell them:
Search through the ravines
and make from the clays
another scorched eagle.


If you cannot, then,
oh, forget her.
I killed her. You too,
kill her!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Mad Blue and Mad Green...
translations.text:
Mad blue and mad green
of flax in stalk and flower.
Dizzy with waves,
the lovely blue-maker dances.


When blue sheds its petals,
the green dancer follows:
clover green, olive green,
and bright lemon green.


What beauty!
What color!


Mild red and fierce red,
rose and bursting carnation.
When the greens surrender,
it leaps like a champion.


They dance one after another;
who can say which is best?
The reds dance so much
they burn in their own ardor.


What madness!
What color!


Yellow comes along,
grand and full of fervor,
and everyone makes way
as if for Agamemnon.


For human and divine alike
the holy radiance dances:
aromatic golden clusters
and flying saffron.


What delirium!
What color!


At last they follow along
after the sun's peacock,
who gathers and carries them
like a father or a thief.


Hand in hand with us,
they were all there; now they're gone:
the world's tale dies
when the Teller dies!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: I Believe in My Heart
translations.text:
I believe in my heart, a fragrant bough
that my Lord shakes like foliage,
perfuming all life with love
and making it blessed.


I believe in my heart, which asks
for nothing because it can dream the highest dream
and embraces all creation in that dream:
immense its dominion!


I believe in my heart, which when it sings
dives into the deep God, wounded and frank,
to rise from the living pool
newborn.


I believe in my heart, which trembles
because He made it, He who troubled the seas,
and in the One who gives Life its orchestrations
like the highest tides.


I believe in my heart, which I wring out
to dye life's canvas
red or pale, and which has made it
a glowing garment.


I believe in my heart, which in the sowing,
through the endless furrow, kept growing.
I believe in my heart, always poured out,
yet never emptied.


I believe in my heart, where the worm
will not bite, for it will blunt death;
I believe in my heart, resting
on the breast of mighty, terrible God.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: When Midnight Came...
translations.text:
When midnight came
and the Child broke into tears,
the hundred beasts awoke,
and the stable came alive.


They drew nearer,
stretched toward the Child
their hundred yearning necks,
like a forest shaken by wind.


An ox lowered its breath to His face
and breathed it out without a sound;
its eyes were tender,
as though full of dew.


A ewe rubbed against Him
with her very soft fleece,
and two little goats, crouching,
licked His hands…


Without noticing, the stable walls
became covered with pheasants and geese,
with roosters and blackbirds.


The pheasants came down,
passing their great colored tails
over the Child;
and the broad-billed geese


arranged the straw for Him;
and the swarm of blackbirds
was a fluttering veil
over the newborn…


And the Virgin, amid horns
and whitish breathing,
went back and forth, bewildered,
unable to catch the Child.


And Joseph came laughing
to help in the confusion.
The stable, shaken,
was like a forest in the wind…
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.
